Mrigal carp (Cirrhinus mrigala) is a large-bodied cyprinid native to the river systems of the Indian subcontinent, where it supports substantial aquaculture and capture fisheries. Recently metamorphosed juveniles are estimated to have a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0005236 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0005236 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of approximately one millimeter observed in congeneric species such as Cirrhinus cirrhosus. This extremely small initial body mass underscores the vulnerability of the early life stages, when free-swimming larvae rely entirely on exogenous feeding following yolk-sac resorption. Under stable hatchery conditions maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the eggs hatch after just 7 days [ab = 7 days], a rapid developmental period that facilitates high survival in productive nursery environments. The subsequent onset of exogenous feeding and the transition through the pelagic larval phase are characterized by accelerated growth rates, as the fingerlings quickly exploit the abundant planktonic resources typical of tropical freshwater ecosystems.

As the fish progress through the fingerling and sub-adult stages, their growth trajectory can be modeled by standard von Bertalanffy curves fitted to mark-recapture data from natural populations. The ultimate total length achieved by this species is 99 centimeters [Li = 99 centimeters], a maximum size that places it among the larger members of the Indian major carp group. An adult body mass of approximately 14,635 grams [Wwi = approximately 14,635 grams] reflects the energetic investment required for this species to attain its large asymptotic size in a productive tropical floodplain habitat. These large dimensions reflect the energetic advantage of a warm, productive habitat that supplies abundant detrital and planktivorous food resources throughout the year. The attainment of such sizes is, however, a gradual process, requiring several years of sustained feeding during the juvenile and sub-adult phases before the growth rate decelerates markedly near the asymptotic upper limit.

The timing of reproductive maturation in Cirrhinus mrigala is closely tied to water temperature, with controlled experiments revealing that females reach puberty at 730 days after birth [tp = 730 days after birth] when maintained at a constant 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. At this developmental stage, the wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 340 grams [Wwp = approximately 340 grams], indicating that reproductive competence is achieved at a relatively modest body size compared to the ultimate asymptote. The corresponding total length at puberty for females is 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters], a dimension that is readily measurable in the field and often used by fisheries biologists to set minimum size limits for harvest. This size at maturation is considerably smaller than the ultimate length of 99 cm [Li = 99 cm], a pattern typical of iteroparous cyprinids that allocate energy to reproduction well before somatic growth is complete. The onset of vitellogenesis and the first spawning event mark the transition from the immature juvenile stage to the reproductively active adult phase.

The life span of Cirrhinus mrigala is notable for its duration, with captive-reared individuals maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] documented to survive for 9,125 days [am = 9,125 days] under optimal conditions; this longevity, equivalent to approximately 25 years, is among the highest recorded for any Indian major carp. Field studies using otolith annuli from wild populations in the Ganges basin have corroborated this extended lifespan, with the oldest sampled individuals consistently exceeding two decades [am = two decades], a duration that is among the longest recorded for any Indian major carp and likely reflects the low natural mortality rates in undisturbed riverine habitats. This long reproductive window allows females to participate in numerous spawning seasons, with each gravid individual capable of producing large numbers of small, adhesive eggs during the monsoon-driven breeding events. The interplay between delayed senescence and iteroparous reproduction is central to the population dynamics of this species. This maximum lifespan of 9,125 days [am = 9,125 days] exceeds that of many other Indian major carps, suggesting a demographic strategy that relies on the reproductive contribution of older, experienced spawners at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

Comparative analyses within the genus Cirrhinus highlight the intermediate life-history strategy of C. mrigala, which exhibits a longer lifespan than the more rapidly maturing Cirrhinus cirrhosus but a shorter maximum length. The ecological role of this species as a benthic detritivore is reflected in its relatively low trophic position and its broad environmental tolerance, attributes that facilitate its integration into polyculture systems across South and Southeast Asia. The larval stage, from first exogenous feeding through the exotrophic transition, constitutes a critical bottleneck where survival depends on prey availability and water quality. Stock enhancement programs routinely assess larval condition indices at the yolk-sac larva stage, monitoring the timing of the switch to active feeding at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] to optimize hatchery protocols. Future research should focus on the heritability of growth parameters, particularly the relationship between length at puberty and ultimate size, and on quantifying the effects of climate change on the thermal regime of monsoon rivers that drive spawning migrations.
